newsitem.title: CONGO: Summary executions in Congo... and boys with guns.
newsitem.headline: Summary executions in Congo... and boys with guns.

text.p: In a corner of the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville, men accused of being spies are given five minutes to explain themselves.
Invariably, witnesses say, their fate is sealed with a bullet to the head or chest -- with a jeering crowd looking on.
In the same part of town, shells and rockets slam into civilian homes sowing death and destruction.
Elsewhere, the rotting body of a schoolboy, his bag still on his back, lies where he fell -- cut down by a stray bullet.

Death in the capital of this former French colony, held hostage by a bloody power struggle between President Pascal Lissouba and his erstwhile Marxist military predecessor, is no respector of persons.
Human rights are just another casualty of war.

"I saw three people executed yesterday," said Guillaume Ngefa, exiled head of the Zairean human rights group AZADHO, who had sought refuge in Brazzaville after fleeing in May in fear of his life across the river from Kinshasa.
"First they were tortured and beaten. Then they were shot," he told Reuters while being evacuated by French forces on Monday.

Ngefa, whose organisation was a thorn in the side of ousted Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, said he had watched at least 20 summary executions in Brazzaville's northern suburbs, stronghold of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia.
Brazzaville's nightmare began on June 5 when the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home during a crackdown on private militias in the run-up to a July 27 presidential election.
"When the fighting started, Sassou's people came round and gave everybody over 13 a gun and told them to fight," he said.
"Every day they go to pick up what they call 'rations' -- of bullets," he added.
Ngefa said that the northern suburbs were solidly behind Sassou Nguesso and all the young men there were Cobras.

He described Sassou Nguesso's forces, who have pushed back soldiers and militia loyal to Lissouba on several fronts, as more disciplined than the regular army. Some former soldiers had even switched sides, joining the Cobras.
Ngefa said that all those people he saw being accused of being spies or infiltrators came from Lissouba's home region in the west -- if not from his tribe.
Before being killed, they were given about five minutes to defend themselves while crowds of local people jeered, he said. Then they were shot in the head or the chest, he added.
Ngefa, who moved around the northern suburbs during the fighting, said that during rocket or shell attacks by Lissouba loyalists, civilians fled from one district to another.
He saw four houses smashed by shells and estimated that the death toll in those attacks was around 18 people.
With medical workers unable to move around freely to collect bodies, most of those killed lie when they fell.
At least 2,000 people were killed in similar ethnic and political clashes in 1993, after a disputed parliamentary election.
This time, some sources talk of hundreds killed -- maybe even several thousand. Nobody really knows.
